text: The accused was charged under Section 302 of the Penal Code 1860 for committing murder.
notes: Section 302 of the Bangladesh Penal Code prescribes the punishment for murder.

text: The magistrate granted bail to the accused under Section 497 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898.
citation: Section 497 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898
notes: Section 497 governs bail in non-bailable offences under BD law.

text: An appeal from an original decree was preferred under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908.
citation: Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908
notes: Section 96 of the CPC allows appeals from original decrees.

text: The tribunal sentenced the offender under Section 9(1) of the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000.
citation: Section 9(1) of the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000
notes: Section 9(1) of the Ain governs punishment for rape.

text: The petition was filed under Section 302A of the Penal Code 1860 for murder conspiracy.
notes: No Section 302A exists in the Bangladesh Penal Code.

text: The police registered the case under Section 512 of the Penal Code 1860.
notes: The Penal Code 1860 only contains 511 sections.

text: The accused was prosecuted under Section 326 of the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000 for grievous hurt.
citation: Section 326 of the Nari O Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain 2000
notes: Section 326 defines grievous hurt in the Penal Code 1860, not Nari O Shishu.

text: A search warrant was issued under Section 100 of the Penal Code 1860 to find the missing child.
notes: Search warrants are issued under Section 100 of the CrPC, not the Penal Code (where Section 100 is about the right of private defence).

text: The prosecution alleged theft under Section 378 of the Penal Code 1860, which prescribes the death penalty for murder.
notes: Section 378 defines theft, but the text misstates its content by linking it to murder/death penalty.

text: The court held that under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, no appeal shall lie from any original decree.
citation: Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908
notes: Section 96 explicitly states that appeals *shall* lie from original decrees, so this misstates the legal content.

text: The charge sheet was submitted under Section 498A of the Penal Code 1860 regarding husband's cruelty.
notes: Section 498A is an Indian Penal Code section and does not exist in the Bangladesh Penal Code.

text: The victim's family filed a case under Section 304B of the Penal Code 1860 for dowry death.
notes: Section 304B (dowry death) is an Indian IPC amendment, not present in the Bangladesh Penal Code.

text: The precedent of State v. Shafiuddin, 54 DLR 21 was cited for definition of common intention.
notes: This is a real judgment of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

text: The landmark ruling in BLAST v. Bangladesh, 55 DLR 313 established guidelines on arrest.
notes: This is a real High Court Division case regarding arrest guidelines.

text: In Rahman v. The State, 80 DLR (AD) 902, the court laid down rules for bail.
notes: No such case or volume (80 DLR AD 902) exists in Bangladeshi law reports.

text: The division bench relied on State v. Shafiuddin, 72 DLR (AD) 55 for case law guidelines.
notes: State v. Shafiuddin is not at 72 DLR AD 55 (it is 54 DLR 21).

text: In BLAST v. Bangladesh, 55 DLR 313, the court held that the death penalty is mandatory for drug trafficking.
notes: BLAST v. Bangladesh (55 DLR 313) is about arbitrary arrest guidelines (Section 54 CrPC), not drug trafficking or the death penalty.

text: The Appellate Division in BLAST v. Bangladesh, 55 DLR 313 held that Section 54 of CrPC requires guidelines.
notes: The 55 DLR 313 judgment was decided by the High Court Division, not the Appellate Division.

text: The Appellate Division in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, AIR 1973 SC 1461 laid down the basic structure doctrine.
citation: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, AIR 1973 SC 1461
notes: Kesavananda Bharati is a landmark decision of the Supreme Court of India, not the Appellate Division of Bangladesh.

text: The court cited Dr. Mohiuddin Farooque v. Bangladesh, 49 DLR (AD) 1 to establish locus standi in public interest litigation.
citation: Dr. Mohiuddin Farooque v. Bangladesh, 49 DLR (AD) 1
notes: This is a real landmark Appellate Division case on public interest standing.
